newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Crude Outlook - sour grades leads the way lower.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Crude Outlook - sour grades leads the way lower.

text.p: The crude oil market in the U.S. is expected to remain swamped with supply this week, underscoring a broadbased sell-off in crude and products which has brought prices down to levels not seen since the end of last summer, traders said.

Leading the way lower for crude grades is the sour sector, with levels Monday in benchmark West Texas Sour/Midland holding at around $2.85 below benchmark West Texas Intermediate/Cushing, having lost about 40 cents last week.

The discount for sour crude versus benchmark has doubled since the start of the year under the weight of heavy supply, lower demand because of a relatively mild winter and a heavy schedule of first quarter refinery turnarounds.
"There is plenty of supply and there has been plenty of supply for some time," said one Texas cash oil trader.
In addition to domestic product, traders saw rising availabilities from the Gulf of Mexico, Canada, Mexico, Iraq and Venezuela.
Glaring sour weakness was best exemplified in the widening of the sour/sweet crude spread, a trend traders expected to continue this week.

The spread between bellwethers West Texas Intermediate/Cushing and West Texas Sour/Midland averaged $1.66 a barrel in January 1997, compared to 90 cents a barrel in January 1996 and just 56 cents a barrel ten years ago.
Meanwhile, outright crude prices have been fluctuating in-line with the products, and could see a change in that influence this week, oil analysts said.
"This could be the week we turn it, and become a gasoline driven market," said Bill O'Grady, oil analayst for A.G. Edwards and Sons in St. Louis.
A key for the gasoline and crude's fortunes will be the inventory data on Tuesday from the American Petroleum Institute, followed by Wednesday's U.S. government data.
"If you see good draw numbers indicating (gasoline) demand has popped-up, then that will probably lift the whole complex," said O'Grady.
He said that spot crude prices have been dominated by the products for some time, allowing the autumn/winter price rally even as the world remained awash in crude.
"The real story has been in refining capacity, not in drilling output. All along there has been plenty of crude in the world," said O'Grady.

Other analysts said the market would remain attuned for any Iraq news, mainly on United Nations inspectors searching for missiles. The regular 60-day sanctions review comes up for U.N. Security Council review next Monday.

Iraqi foreign minister Mohammed Saeed al-Sahaf is scheduled to arrive in New York Tuesday evening in an effort to lobby U.N. members for a lifting of sanctions clamped on Baghdad six years ago after it invaded Kuwait.

Iraq has been allowed to sell limited supplies of crude since December 10 under the oil-for-food deal, a humanitarian exception to the sanctions permitting Baghdad to buy food and aid for suffering civilians with oil receipts.

The U.N. sanctions committee on Iraq was to meet this week and formalize expedited procedures to speed delivery of food to Iraq. Even though millions of dollars in oil receipts have been collected since the deal started, imports of supplies have been sluggish, angering Baghdad.
